Banchan / Heritage

Kongnamul Muchim Seasoned Soybean Sprouts

Soybean sprouts are the banchan that appears at nearly every Korean meal, including the grill table's — crunchy, nutty, cheap, and ready in fifteen minutes.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4–6 as banchan

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the everyday namul. Soybean sprouts are the banchan that appears at nearly every Korean meal, including the grill table's — crunchy, nutty, cheap, and ready in fifteen minutes. The whole technique is one law: cook them uncovered so the bean's raw, grassy edge cooks off with the steam, then dress them while warm so they drink the sesame and garlic. This is also the parent recipe for the whole muchim/namul family on this site (#B06, #B17): blanch, shock, season is the pattern.

The sprouts

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Pick through the sprouts once — the loose yellow hulls float off in the rinse, and any browned bean ends should go. Ten seconds per handful; the bowl's cleanliness is visible in the finished banchan.
  • Set a colander in the sink and the seasoning bowl beside it; sprouts go from pot to colander to bowl without pause.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Salted water at a full boil, sprouts in, uncovered — the law of this record. Six minutes at a steady boil, stirred once. Checkpoint — a test sprout: the tail is fully tender (no string) and the bean is just soft with the faintest bite, and the raw-grassy smell from the pot's first minute has cooked off entirely — that smell leaving is exactly what the uncovered boil lets happen.
  2. 02
    Drain well — really well, a full minute in the colander, shaking — and turn the hot sprouts into the seasoning bowl while they still steam. Checkpoint — the residual heat is doing the garlic's cooking: thirty seconds after tossing, the bowl smells nutty-savory, not sharp-raw.
  3. 03
    Toss with everything, taste, adjust — the banchan should read sesame-first, salt behind, a clean crunch. Checkpoint — the eating test with rice and any grilled meat from this site's M-list: the sprouts reset the palate between rich bites. That is the banchan's job description, and this bowl does it as well as anything on the table. Chef’s Note — the covered-versus-uncovered boil is the difference between the two sprout cultures of the Korean kitchen: uncovered (this record) boils the mucky, beany aromatics away for a clean, salad-like banchan; the covered school (the sujebi and kongnamul-guk school) traps those same aromatics deliberately for a fuller, earthier soup-side flavor. Neither is wrong; they are two dishes using one vegetable, and the uncovered road is the one that belongs at the grill table.

The seasoning

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Beany, muddy tasteCovered boilUncovered, full six minutes
Watery, diluted seasoningUnder-drainedThe full minute draining, shake the colander
Limp tailsOvercooked or sprouts oldSix minutes at a rolling boil; buy firm, white tails
Sharp raw garlicDressed after coolingDress while steaming — the heat cooks it

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Keeps 2–3 days refrigerated and holds crunch better than most banchan; refresh with a few drops of sesame oil at serving.
  • Variations: a spoon of gochugaru for the red build; the spinach (#B06) and bellflower (#B17) records run this same blanch-and-dress pattern; day-after sprouts folded into bibimbap or fried rice.
